# AI Could Do My First Job. Not My Last.

This blog post was originally published on PIIE senior fellow Jason Furman's Econvitals.org website and republished here with permission. Furman wrote the blog post with assistance from AI (see his website for details).

Warning: This is different from what my other Occasional Posts will be. It is longer, more personal and more opinionated, with almost no data and no charts. But it also addresses some important issues, so I hope you read it. Or if you're busy, paste it into an AI and have it produce a summary and critique at whatever length or depth works for you.

I want to talk about my comment to Neil Irwin about the White House Council of Economic Advisers (CEA) when Econvitals was released: "If I were running the CEA today and had a choice between 20 staff members who had a combination of current Ph.D.s and future Ph.D.s versus the AI systems that we have today, I would somewhat regretfully and sadly choose the AI systems." It would be fair to say the reaction to it was generally negative, including from many friends and former colleagues. I confess that makes me a bit mad and a bit sad.

The mad is entirely at myself for choosing a provocative example in order to stimulate a conversation, when instead it backfired and closed off the conversation. And the sad is because we are facing some very difficult and challenging issues, at least in certain pockets of the labor market , and I worry that unrealistic denials of risks and tradeoffs—albeit not certainties—could get in the way of honestly confronting what we are facing. At a moment like this we need realism, honesty and a willingness to make difficult choices.

I am not saying my view is definitely right, just that it is not so obviously wrong. In this post I will try to do a better job explaining why and what it might mean. I am going to be granular about CEA because I think it is a useful thought experiment, in the ways it does and does not generalize to other organizations.

## The Council of Economic Advisers: An Amazing Group of Thirty-Five Humans That Could Be Mostly Replicated by About Ten Humans Plus AI

So let me get to my specific claim: I believe that most of what CEA did when I ran it could now be done by about ten people. Which means AI could replace much of what a group of bright people, from recent college graduates to seasoned academics, could do. So my 20-person comment to Neil may have understated the case. (Later on I will get to the different and more important question: not reproducing what we did but figuring out what to do in the future, which shifts the issue from whether AI could replace people to whether it should.)

A bit of background. CEA is like an in-house think tank that provides economic advice to the President and the administration, as well as a set of public reports including the Economic Report of the President . It is a small, scrappy staff of about 35 people, most of them not permanent government employees—including about ten Senior Economists, many of whom are professors on leave from universities, and another roughly ten incredibly talented and hard-working junior staff who are often headed to or in the middle of Ph.D. programs.

When I ran the Council of Economic Advisers from mid-2013 to the beginning of 2017 we produced dozens of reports that helped contribute to the conversation on everything from competition to male employment to how to extract the signal from macroeconomic data , not to mention contributing to myriad policy issues including Medicare payments, criminal justice reform and the Clean Power Plan. None of that would have been possible without the ideas, initiative and execution of the people who worked there.

AI on its own or AI with just me directing it could not replace all of that. As I told Neil, "You would need people at CEA to interact in meetings, to talk to the press, talk to Congress." But CEA would not need nearly as many humans for just these tasks.

AI is an outstanding research assistant and is doing increasingly sophisticated economic reasoning and analysis. But humans would still play a critical role. If I were running an AI-intensive CEA with only a skeleton staff, I would expect the remaining humans to be in frequent conversation with economists and policy wonks, both across the administration and outside it, to challenge our ideas, get new ones, share our results and try to persuade people. This is not complete automation. But it is AI doing most implementation.

## The Messy Reality of Who AI Can and Cannot Replace

My expertise on these issues comes only partly from my time as Chair under President Obama. Perhaps even more relevant is what I learned and did as a CEA staffer under President Clinton. At that earlier time my job was mostly performing short analyses, tracking macroeconomic data and writing short memos on it, drafting reports, working on the administration's forecast, and working with Joe Stiglitz and then Janet Yellen on their speeches. It was amazing and challenging work. I would not be the person I am today if I had not gone through that intensive experience and the mentorship I got from them. But I look back on that time and truly believe that AI—guided and directed by Stiglitz, Yellen and other more senior people—could easily do 95 percent of what I did then. And the other 5 percent was staffing Stiglitz on trips, doing things like getting him a new tie when he spilled on the old one.

A few people responded to my argument with claims that the CEA Chair might even be more replaceable than many of the people who work for them. It might sound just, but it is also wrong. Jason as Chair could not be replaced by AI but Jason as junior staffer could be. That is not because Jason as Chair was smarter or better than Jason as junior staffer. It is because the task mix for the Chair is mostly about being in meetings, briefing the President, testifying to Congress, making speeches, reaching out to discuss issues with academics and the like—those just are not jobs that an AI can do. In contrast, the task mix for a junior staffer—and even for some senior economists with decades of experience—is mostly doing analysis and writing on a computer and emailing it to the people who use it. That could be done by AI.

The reality gets very messy in ways that measures of AI exposure are unlikely to capture. For example, the effect of AI on employment at the National Economic Council (NEC), where I did two stints, could be quite different from its impact on employment at CEA. The NEC and CEA are both White House economic advisers and employ similar types of people, especially in the junior ranks. But the NEC is a more strategic and political organization that manages the policy process and is heavily involved in the passage and implementation of policy. Most junior staffers at the NEC are probably safer from AI than even more senior staffers at CEA, not because NEC staffers are smarter and more talented than CEA staffers but because much of the job of NEC staffers is running meetings, building coalitions and working with a wide range of units to implement policies—none of which can be done by AI.

So the issue of who AI can replace is not one of who is more virtuous or smarter or better or even who is more senior or more junior. It is about what the nature of the job is. AI poses more of a threat to some of the smartest people in the academy, like mathematicians , than to people in many other disciplines, although I have heard a number of colleagues in different disciplines wonder if their days as active researchers are numbered.

## Don't Underestimate How Capable AI Is: It Can Write Decent Economics Papers, Very Good Briefings and Excellent Blogs With Basically No Human Input

Part of the disconnect in the discourse is that people have different understandings of the current capabilities of AI. More and more people understand them, but I still sometimes hear people talking about AI hallucinations or how it repackages Wikipedia. These might have been true of badly used, weaker AI models a year or two ago, but they are barely relevant for understanding agentic AI today.

To understand it better, as an experiment I built an engine I call Paperwright . It takes a short prompt and spends two to ten hours turning it into an economics paper, drawing on a multi-step agent process that includes researchers, writers, fact checkers and referees. For example, I entered "data centers and electricity prices" and about six hours later I got this 65-page paper , which has a mathematical model, an analysis of county-level data drawn from Environmental Protection Agency permit records, the Energy Information Administration and other sources, references and appendices, plus a replication package . I don't think the paper is a great contribution to knowledge, and it should not be published in even a mid-level journal, but if it were a senior thesis it would probably get a grade in the Summa range at Harvard. And if you think that paper is wild, check out this one , produced with a one-word prompt: "Triffin."

I also created Blogwright as an experiment to see if AI could write think tank-style blogs that explain things, organize and summarize data, or make a case. The results, in my judgment, would be among the better versions of the genre at the better think tanks, on topics including the case for reviving the Premium Tax Credit , how work from home has changed the labor market for women , why the budget problem is that taxes are too low and why the budget problem is that spending is too high .

These blogs are better than what a chatbot could do today, given the ways I have architected the multi-step process for writing them and the links to over one hundred data sources. But I expect even a simple prompt into a chatbot will do better than this in a year or two. Moreover, what started as an experiment has turned into an input into my thinking—on many topics I would rather get up to speed with an AI-generated blog post than anything written by humans, which might be out of date, not match my interests or have inaccurate or misleading numbers (AI, used properly, can make fewer mistakes than people).

I also created Briefwright to write briefings for me on various topics, ranging from literature reviews on audit studies to analysis of the wealth effect in supporting current consumption to an evaluation of the climate forecasting track record . None of them are fully reliable from beginning to end, but all of them are informative and generative as an input to my own thinking and writing.

Econvitals itself is built the same way. Almost every email you receive from it was written by AI. I don't approve, read or edit them before they go out. I iterated on the prompts, designed the pool of charts they draw on and architected the overall system. The exceptions are a paragraph I write in Morning Notes about a chart I select and design, and these Occasional Posts . The emails have been timely, reasonably comprehensive and generally accurate.

But I also expect my own posts will be more interesting than anything the AI writes. I don't say that to brag about myself; most days the Morning Note links to two pieces it selects as interesting by different people and organizations, and those are also more interesting than anything written by AI. As are innumerable other human-written pieces it does not link to.

Some of the AI-generated papers, blogs and briefings are cutting-edge. Some need significant work and have big deficiencies that need to be remedied by humans. And some of the longer papers might even be garbage. But all of them were done by AI in 2026 (it will get better), by systems I architected (I'm decent at this but many people are much better), and with basically no human input or iteration beyond architecting the system and then entering a simple prompt.
